items.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996
items.q: you know, the Dorsey Brothers and quite a few of the bands broke up.

ctx.x: Yeah, but when it got into the bop period for instance, it became a lot of times much quicker tempos and less danceable.

I think there was economic considerations that went on. There weren’t, for a long time there weren’t records. People had to go. Sometimes they drove a hundred, a hundred fifty miles to go see a band you know. So this had a lot to do with the live aspect of performance in that time. But when Woody’s band broke up in late ‘46, records were becoming quite commonplace. The bands were becoming very expensive to field, the economy was not good then, and there was a whole combination of elements. Woody’s band was doing…

know, the Dorsey Brothers and quite a few of the bands broke up. It was really the end of an era. And television had a great deal to do with it, so there was a whole bunch of factors, I mean as I see it, that came into play then.
